title: Subnetting & VLSM
summary: Split one network into smaller pieces. Learn masks, CIDR, host counts, and VLSM — the tool that makes every address count.

blocks.markdown:
**Subnetting** divides one IP network into smaller logical networks called **subnets**.

- A single large network wastes addresses and creates one big broadcast domain.
- Subnets isolate traffic, improve security, and match each segment to its real size.
- A **subnet mask** tells devices which bits identify the network and which identify the host.
- **VLSM** lets each subnet use a different mask size — no address left unused.

See [ipv4-addressing](ipv4-addressing) for IP basics.

blocks.subTitle: Why subnet?
blocks.markdown:
Reasons to split a network:

- **Reduce broadcast traffic** — a broadcast hits every device on the subnet, not the whole building.
- **Isolate segments** — HR and engineering traffic stays separate.
- **Conserve IPs** — allocate only what each group needs.
- **Match physical layout** — one subnet per floor or VLAN.

**CIDR** (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) writes a network as `address/prefix`. The prefix is the number of **network bits** in the mask.

- `192.168.1.0/24` — 24 network bits, 8 host bits.
- `10.0.0.0/8` — 8 network bits, 24 host bits.
- Smaller prefix = larger network. `/8` holds millions of hosts; `/30` holds just two.

CIDR replaced the old class A/B/C system, letting you create subnets of any size.

blocks.subTitle: Common prefixes at a glance
blocks.markdown:
Quick reference — prefix, mask, and usable host count.

| Prefix | Subnet Mask | Usable Hosts |
|---|---|---|
| /24 | 255.255.255.0 | 254 |
| /25 | 255.255.255.128 | 126 |
| /26 | 255.255.255.192 | 62 |
| /27 | 255.255.255.224 | 30 |
| /28 | 255.255.255.240 | 14 |
| /30 | 255.255.255.252 | 2 |

Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2 (subtract network and broadcast addresses).

A **subnet mask** is a 32-bit number where all network bits are 1 and all host bits are 0.

- AND the IP with the mask → you get the **network address**.
- The host portion is whatever's left over.

Example: IP `192.168.1.130`, mask `255.255.255.128` (`/25`).
- Mask in binary ends `10000000`; the host part is the lower 7 bits.
- Network address = `192.168.1.128`; host = `.130 − .128 = 2`.

When you borrow **n** bits from the host portion to create subnets:

- **Number of subnets** = 2^n
- **Hosts per subnet** = 2^(remaining host bits) − 2

Subtracting 2 removes the **network address** (all host bits = 0) and the **broadcast address** (all host bits = 1) — neither can be assigned to a device.

blocks.subTitle: Network and broadcast addresses
blocks.markdown:
Every subnet has two reserved addresses:

- **Network address** — first address, all host bits = 0. Identifies the subnet itself.
- **Broadcast address** — last address, all host bits = 1. A packet sent here reaches every device in the subnet.

For `192.168.1.64/26` (64 addresses, host bits = 6):
- Network: `192.168.1.64`
- Broadcast: `192.168.1.127`
- Usable: `.65` → `.126` (62 addresses).

**Divide `192.168.1.0/24` into four equal subnets.**

Borrow 2 bits from host → prefix becomes `/26`. Each subnet has 64 addresses, 62 usable.

| Subnet | Network Addr | Broadcast |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 192.168.1.0 | 192.168.1.63 |
| 2 | 192.168.1.64 | 192.168.1.127 |
| 3 | 192.168.1.128 | 192.168.1.191 |
| 4 | 192.168.1.192 | 192.168.1.255 |

Step: 256 ÷ 4 subnets = 64 addresses each. Subnets start at 0, 64, 128, 192.

**VLSM** (Variable Length Subnet Masking) lets each subnet use a **different prefix length** — sized to actual need.

- Without VLSM all subnets are the same size, wasting addresses in small segments.
- With VLSM: give a 50-host segment `/26` (62 hosts), a 10-host segment `/28` (14 hosts), a point-to-point link `/30` (2 hosts).
- Allocate largest subnets first, then fit smaller ones into the gaps.

VLSM is standard in modern networks; requires classless routing (OSPF, BGP).

blocks.subTitle: Why it matters
blocks.markdown:
VLSM in action: allocate `10.0.0.0/24` to three segments.

<<< Image: clean network diagram, white background, blue/grey palette. Three labeled boxes: 'Dept A (50 hosts) /26 → 10.0.0.0–10.0.0.63', 'Dept B (12 hosts) /28 → 10.0.0.64–10.0.0.79', 'Link (2 hosts) /30 → 10.0.0.80–10.0.0.83'. Remaining space labeled 'Unused: 10.0.0.84–10.0.0.255'. Arrows from parent block to each sub-block. >>>

- Fixed subnetting would give all three a `/26`, wasting 48 addresses on Dept B and 62 on the link.

**Supernetting** is the reverse of subnetting — combine contiguous smaller blocks into one larger prefix to shrink routing tables.

- `192.168.0.0/24` + `192.168.1.0/24` → `192.168.0.0/23` (one route for both).
- Also called **route aggregation** or **route summarization**.
- Routers advertise one prefix instead of many; less memory, faster lookups. See [routing](routing).

Requires that the blocks are contiguous and aligned on a power-of-two boundary.

Common mistakes:

- **Off-by-two on host count.** Always subtract 2 (network + broadcast). A /26 gives 62 usable, not 64.
- **Overlapping subnets.** Allocating ranges that share addresses breaks routing silently.
- **Not aligning to boundaries.** A subnet must start at a multiple of its block size (e.g. /26 blocks start at 0, 64, 128, 192 — not 10).
- **VLSM order.** Always carve out the largest subnet first, then smaller ones fit into remaining space.

blocks.subTitle: Hosts in a /26
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How many usable hosts are in a /26 subnet?**

A /26 has 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 addresses. Subtract 2 (network + broadcast) = **62 usable hosts**. The network address is .0 (or whatever the block starts at) and the broadcast is .63.

blocks.subTitle: What is CIDR?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is CIDR and why did it replace classful addressing?**

CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) writes a network as `IP/prefix`, where the prefix is the number of network bits. It replaced rigid class A/B/C blocks — you can now allocate exactly the size needed, reducing waste and letting route aggregation shrink internet routing tables.

blocks.subTitle: Why use VLSM?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why use VLSM instead of fixed-size subnets?**

Fixed subnets force every segment to the same size — a 2-host point-to-point link wastes 60 addresses in a /26. VLSM sizes each subnet to its real need, so no addresses are wasted. It requires classless routing protocols (OSPF, BGP) that carry the prefix with each route advertisement.

**Q: Find the network and broadcast address of `10.1.1.100/27`.**

A /27 block is 32 addresses. 100 ÷ 32 = 3 remainder 4 → block starts at 96. **Network: `10.1.1.96`; Broadcast: `10.1.1.127`.**
